notes.meaning: Spring was the usual time for ancient armies to go to war, because the cold winter rains were over and travel was easier. Joab led the army out to defeat the Ammonites and surrounded their capital city of Rabbah, while David stayed behind in Jerusalem. The writer focuses on the public history of the kingdom and leaves out David's sin with Bathsheba, which happened during this time.

David arrived after the city fell and took the gold crown from the Ammonite king or their idol, Milcom. It was decorated with jewels and weighed about seventy-five pounds, which was too heavy to wear for long, so it was likely held or suspended over David's head. The valuable spoils of war taken from the city were later set aside to help build the temple of the Lord.

David brought the captives out of the city and put them to hard labor with building tools like saws, iron picks, and axes. He placed the conquered people into forced service to quarry stone and cut wood across Ammon before leading his army home. This secured peace on Israel's eastern border and provided workers for future royal projects.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars read the Hebrew text as saying David executed the Ammonite captives with cruel methods rather than putting them to work with construction tools.

notes.meaning: Another war started when the Philistines challenged Israel near the town of Gezer. A brave warrior named Sibbecai stepped forward and killed Sippai, who came from an ancient family known for being giants. God gave his people victory, proving that Israel could overcome huge enemies even without David fighting on the front lines.

During another clash with the Philistines, Elhanan killed Lahmi, the brother of Goliath from Gath. Lahmi carried a massive spear with a heavy shaft as thick as a weaver's beam. While the earlier record in Samuel suffered a small copying error that left out words, Chronicles makes clear that Elhanan killed Goliath's brother rather than Goliath himself.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many critical scholars think the original story credited Elhanan with killing Goliath, and that the author of Chronicles changed the text to protect David's famous victory.

notes.meaning: A giant warrior from Gath came out to fight with a rare physical condition, having six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot. His unusual size and extra digits made him look terrifying to anyone who faced him. Yet physical size and strength are nothing when standing against the living God.

The giant shouted insults against the army of Israel, just as Goliath had done years before. David's nephew Jonathan was not afraid and struck him down in battle. Those who mock God and his people ultimately bring about their own ruin.

These four giant champions from Gath were completely defeated through David's leadership and the courage of his men. David had inspired a new generation of faithful fighters who could slay giants just as he had done in his youth. God gave his people full victory over their oldest and most fearsome enemies.
